what: The score combines exact insertion distance with three candidate-priority signals: Clarke–Wright affinity to the current route, affinity to a nearby unassigned customer that can still fit afterward, and mild preference for distant customers. Capacity terms reward filling the route and penalize residual capacity that cannot be closely matched by one remaining demand. It uses the supplied distance matrix, takes O(len(route) + len(unassigned)) time per call, and O(1) extra space.
why: The route-affinity term favors geographically coherent routes while being less dependent on the current ordering, which is useful because intra-route 2-opt may later reorder the route. Future affinity encourages admitting spatially compatible pairs, while the packing terms address the substantial capacity pressure and heterogeneous demands visible in the representative instances. The coefficients keep immediate insertion cost dominant rather than treating the look-ahead signals as a cost-to-go estimate. Limitations include its one-customer approximation to capacity packability, repeated linear scans for every evaluated position, and fixed coefficients that may require validation across instance families.
